content: The Fc fragment of IgA receptor (FCAR) is a gene in humans that encodes the transmembrane receptor FcαRI, also referred to as CD89 (Cluster of Differentiation 89). FcαRI specifically binds to the heavy-chain constant region of Immunoglobulin A (IgA) antibodies. This receptor is expressed on the surface of myeloid lineage cells, such as neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, and eosinophils. However, it is absent from intestinal macrophages and is not expressed on mast cells. FcαRI is involved in both pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory immune responses, depending on the state of the IgA molecules it binds. The receptor undergoes a process called inside-out signaling to become primed for ligand binding, while outside-in signaling, which occurs after ligand binding, requires its association with the Fc receptor gamma chain (FcR γ-chain). Although FcαRI belongs to the Fc receptor immunoglobulin superfamily, its primary structure is more similar to receptors in the leukocyte receptor cluster (LRC). The FCAR gene is located on chromosome 19, in contrast to other Fc receptor family members, which are encoded on chromosome 1. Interestingly, while FCAR homologs exist in several species, there is no equivalent gene in mice. The structure of FcαRI includes an α-chain composed of two extracellular domains (EC1 and EC2) arranged at a right angle, a transmembrane domain, and an intracellular domain. However, the α-chain alone cannot mediate signaling in response to IgA binding. For signaling to occur, FcαRI must associate with a dimeric FcR γ-chain, which contains immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) at its ends. These ITAMs are critical for transmitting signals into the cell. Two alleles of the FCAR gene, which differ by a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP), encode FcαRI molecules with distinct signaling capabilities. This SNP results in either a serine (Ser248) or glycine (Gly248) residue at position 248 in the intracellular domain of FcαRI. FcαRI molecules with Gly248 exhibit enhanced signaling for the production and release of interleukin-6 (IL-6), even in the absence of FcR γ-chain association, compared to those with Ser248. Additionally, alternative splicing of the FCAR transcript generates ten mRNA variants, which encode different isoforms of FcαRI. Inside-out signaling is a prerequisite for FcαRI to bind IgA with increased affinity. This priming process is initiated when cytokines, signaling the presence of an infection, bind to their receptors on FcαRI-expressing cells. This activates the kinase PI3K, which in turn activates p38 and protein kinase C (PKC). Together with protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A), these molecules dephosphorylate the Serine 263 residue (Ser263) on the intracellular domain of the FcαRI α-chain. This dephosphorylation event primes FcαRI for IgA binding. Notably, this priming process does not require FcαRI to associate with the FcR γ-chain but does depend on cytoskeletal organization. Once primed, FcαRI binds IgA through its EC1 domain, which interacts with the hinge region between the CH2 and CH3 domains of the IgA Fc region. The signaling and cellular responses triggered by FcαRI depend on the state of the IgA molecules it binds. When IgA immune complexes bind to multiple FcαRI molecules, a pro-inflammatory response is initiated. This involves the activation of Src family kinases, such as Lyn, which phosphorylate the ITAMs of the FcR γ-chain. The tyrosine kinase Syk then docks at the phosphorylated ITAMs, initiating downstream signaling pathways involving PI3K and phospholipase C-γ (PLC-γ). These signaling cascades lead to various pro-inflammatory responses, including cytokine release, phagocytosis, respiratory bursts, antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, production of reactive oxygen species, and antigen presentation. Despite its association with ITAMs, which typically mediate activation, FcαRI can also function as an inhibitory receptor. This occurs through a process known as inhibitory ITAM signaling (ITAMi), which results in anti-inflammatory responses. When FcαRI binds monomeric, non-antigen-bound IgA (the predominant form in serum), the resulting signals inhibit other activating receptors, such as FcγR and FcεRI. In this scenario, Lyn partially phosphorylates the ITAMs of the FcR γ-chain, leading to the recruitment of Src homology region 2 domain-containing phosphatase-1 (SHP-1). SHP-1, a tyrosine phosphatase, coordinates the anti-inflammatory response by preventing the phosphorylation of other receptors, thereby maintaining immune homeostasis in the absence of pathogens. This anti-inflammatory role of monomeric IgA-FcαRI binding has potential therapeutic implications, as demonstrated in transgenic mouse models of allergic asthma. Targeting FcαRI with anti-FcαRI Fab antibodies, which mimic monomeric IgA binding, reduced the infiltration of inflammatory leukocytes into airway tissue. The secreted form of IgA (sIgA), a homodimer secreted across epithelial barriers such as the gut lining, has limited ability to bind FcαRI due to steric hindrance. This is caused by a portion of the cleaved polymeric Ig receptor, which facilitates sIgA secretion into the gut lumen, obscuring part of the FcαRI binding site. However, the precursor to sIgA, dimeric IgA (dIgA), binds FcαRI with similar affinity to monomeric IgA. Secreted IgA plays a crucial role in preventing immune responses to commensal gut microbes. Accordingly, intestinal macrophages do not express FcαRI. However, during mucosal tissue invasion by pathogenic bacteria, neutrophils expressing FcαRI can bind and phagocytose dIgA-opsonized bacteria. FcαRI also plays a significant role in neutrophil-mediated killing of tumor cells. When FcαRI-expressing neutrophils encounter IgA-opsonized tumor cells, they not only perform antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity but also release cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), which promote further neutrophil migration to the site of the tumor. The FCAR gene has been shown to interact with FCGR1A, another Fc receptor gene.
